Criminal Code

The house resumed, from Monday, May 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner that Bill C-150, to amend the Criminal Code, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act, the Prisons and Reformatories Act and to make certain consequential amendments to the Combines Investigation Act, the Customs Tariff and the National Defence Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, after all the tenseness we have been experiencing during the past week and even for several weeks, I am ever so pleased to come back, on third reading, to the main points on which we have been and are still insisting so strongly.
Mr. Speaker, yesterday we had the opportunity to hear-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and his Parliamentary Secretary, the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Cantin), summed up their views on the omnibus bill yesterday.
They mentioned in particular the fight we put up against the committee report. Mr. Speaker, in reading over what they said, I noticed the tremendous shortcomings in the arguments brought forward by the spokesmen for the Department of Justice.
In my remarks, I would like to point out those shortcomings and prove that even if all the amendments we introduced were defeated, it remains nevertheless that, in my opinion, we are still right. We are still fighting for a good cause and we would like our arguments to be listened to again seriously.
We would like precisely to refer to the very comments of the Minister of Justice who said

yesterday that he had been through a full and searching debate.
Mr. Speaker, we wish to thank the minister from the bottom of our hearts for his complimentary remarks to us.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

The Minister of Justice or those gossip-mongers who even took the liberty of cutting in, like the hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane) and the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain)?
Mr. Speaker, the minister himself said there had been a full debate; we put some life into it because life was what we wanted to save. We set our minds, our hearts and our souls to this task, and it has been a full debate. You cannot blame anybody for looking after his own interest.
The minister said also that it was a searching debate. Is it the minister who was right, or those members who saw red and forgot to reason and make really acceptable judgments, not only for us because we are members of the Ralliement Creditiste, but for the whole population? I quote the exact words of the minister:
In answering that remark may I say what ministers often say, namely, that we have had a full and searching debate-and I think I can say that with some justification.
We therefore thank the minister for his comments about us. He also recognized that we had made a fine contribution to this debate for which he is grateful. We thank him sincerely for thinking so and I am again quoting the minister who stated yesterday: There have been serious and deep differences of opinion on certain aspects of this proposed legislation. I listened to those opinions with great feeling because I know how sincere and profound are the convictions of members in some quarters of the house, particularly those opinions that are related to measures that affect private morals and the concept of life and death.

I would advise the hon. member for Matane and the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres to refer to the minister if they want to have a high opinion on the Ralliement creditiste.
Mr. Speaker, once again I congratulate the minister on viewing our contribution to the debate in that light.
However, when he states that it is the great majority of the people who support the abortion amendments to the Criminal Code, he is mistaken. Nevertheless, on hearing his statement yesterday, I felt he was showing much feeling, much sincerity. So much in fact that I read between the lines because of the numerous restrictions he made, that he was personally opposed to it and that he was abiding by a commitment already taken and which he felt compelled to fulfil. That is what you can notice when you read between the lines of what the minister told us yesterday.
With the support of a strong majority, we cast doubts, right from the beginning, on the validity of the amendment. If we were just expressing the opinion of a small minority with regard to the idology concerned here, Mr. Speaker, we would not have insisted so much to express our views on the omnibus bill.
We did it because we were convinced that we represented the majority, whereas the minister contends that the government does. He has perhaps forgotten to consider the people who took the trouble to write, send petitions, attend committee meetings-even those of the committee on justice and legal affairs- to express their point of view. When he says that the majority wants such a thing, the minister, I believe, labours under a complete delusion, and I would like to mention other evidence I received yesterday on the approach taken by people belonging to constituencies other than those of hon. members of the Ralliement creditiste.
I received a letter from the constituency of the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain), which shows that the majority of the Canadian people, even outside the constituencies represented by the Ralliement creditiste, think as we do. And this is why we proclaim so insistently that our position is justified.
The letter addressed to me yesterday reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
Several citizens in Champlain riding told me that you had consulted a number of people with regard to the omnibus bill and more particularly
Criminal Code
with regard to the amendments affecting abortion and homosexuality.
You will find rather strange that a voter not of your own riding should write to you to congratulate you and encourage you to hold your position in respect of this anti-natural and out-ofdate bill. I live in the Trois-Rivieres riding and I must tell you that the position taken by our representative at Ottawa does not reflect the opinion of the majority of his voters. I belong to various social clubs, such as the Knight of Columbus, the Kiwanis and others... and I am in a position to tell you that our member (Mr. Mongrain) did not consult us with regard to these amendments to the Criminal Code.
Yet, he conducted a thorough survey when his political future was at stake. He thinks perhaps that it was more important than the right to live.
If I am writing this letter to you it is to make you understand that in the constituency of Trois-Rivieres people are not different from elsewhere and that we recognize that every human being has a right to live. We also believe that moral values must be carefully safeguarded. It is difficult for us to understand the position of our member in this regard. Since he is a fluent speaker, it seems to me he will never have a better opportunity to speak up.
It is precisely for his oratory talent that he was elected and he knows it, but he should keep in mind that the tongue should never be more active than the brain.
The situation is lamentable, Mr. Matte; not only is the government unable to provide Canadians with a decent living but it actually violates the most sacred rights.
Four years under such irresponsible careerists will seem long and diflicult to us.
But as long as there are conscientious people like you and members of your party, we hope that a day will come when we will be less ashamed to live in Canada.
Carry on your good work!
Canadianly yours.
This letter is signed by a constituent in the riding of Trois-Rivieres. If someone has some doubts about its authenticity I will gladly show it to them and even to the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres.
Mr. Speaker, this is one of the many examples of what is happening in other areas of the country, other than those specifically represented here by the members of the Ralliement creditiste. This letter reflects an attitude we are familiar with. That is why I chose it; it truly expresses the beliefs of the population as a whole.

On many occasions, I have asked the same question since the beginning of hhis debate. We have been asked where the bill comes from. Not so long ago-

Not so long ago, a man who today is the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) was appointed Minister of Justice and undertook the recasting of the Criminal Code which reflects the laws of present day society.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. parliamentary secretary to the hon. Minister of Justice for having answered so candidly and with so much naivete the questions which 1 have asked myself since the moment the omnibus bill was mentioned.
The hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Cantin) was also speaking about freedom. He told us-and I am going to quote him exactly, to be sure that I am not speaking in vain, and to assure the house that the fight which we
Criminal Code
led was not useless, that it was not filibustering, but a fight for freedom-and I quote:
The philosophy of this bill is simply this; in a society which, because of the social order which controls more and more the individual, interferes with his liberty, our legislation must be redrafted in order to respect to a greater extent individual freedom.
Mr. Speaker, since the French wording of this paragraph is of a rather doubtful quality, we might advise our good friend, Mr. Amedee Gaudreault, to write an article out of it.
Anyhow, I finally understood what the parliamentary secretary meant: that the law promotes individual freedom.
If the problem under study were not as serious, I would feel inclined either to laugh or to cry over it-I do not know exactly what. That is precisely what we have been trying to prove for weeks: individual freedom must be safeguarded. In order to do so, however, it is extremely important to start by protecting the individual from the very moment he is conceived. Individual freedom? Granted! Let us have laws to protect individual freedom, but let us first ask who is the individual. That is the important thing.
Mr. Speaker, all human lives have an equal value. It is not because one is Minister of Justice, parliamentary secretary or Prime Minister, that one has more personal value than the blacksmith, the farmer or the hon. member for Champlain.
If we agree that all human lives have an equal value, I cannot see why we should then ignore the individual in his mother's womb. It is up to us, it seems to me to protect individual freedom. Those who try to prove that through those amendments to the Criminal Code, individual freedom will be better protected, will not get away with such platitudes. Once again, leave them to "Amedee".
Mr. Speaker, at this point we would like to draw the attention of the house to the new amendment we intend to move in order that there might be more time to study the question.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin):
That the word "now" be left out, and the words "this day six months" be added at the end of the question.
Mr. Speaker, all human lives are of equal value, even if skills and talents vary from one person to another. All human lives have an intrinsic value. That is the basis of our concept of justice, because all human beings

Criminal Code
have equal rights. Everyone is equal before the law, everyone has the same right to life. Such right does not depend on physical or intellectual perfection. That we must strive to understand. Even the ugliest person in the world has a right to justice, whatever this person's physical development or mental state.
The life of a widow or of a disabled person has the same value as that of a normal one, and the life of the retarded child or of the infant too young to understand is no less precious than that of a genius.
We must therefore recognize the full value of the child in his mother's womb, as well as his full right to life as a human being. Such is the freedom of the individual, which spreads over every instant of the life span, from the very beginning of the existence of a human being. Any human being has a right to be protected, even during his embryonary stage. He has the same right to be protected as the child already born; his right to live must be protected and respected as far as possible.
Could we justify abortion when a baby might be born with a malformation? Only if we can justify the killing of malformed babies after birth.
Can we justify abortion in the case of a child conceived out of wedlock? Only if we can justify the killing of illegitimate babies in their crib.
Can we justify abortion because the child will be a heavy burden for the mother and her family? That is the argument of the New Democratic party. We can justify such an abortion only if we can justify infanticide for the same reason.

If a human being has any rights at all, Mr. Speaker, the most important one, in my view, is the right to life. Without it, he has none. The right to life is the first one on which all other rights depend. That is implicit in any declaration of human rights, but the proposed amendments to legislation dealing with abortion do not recognize this fact.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights recognizes that everyone has the right to life, liberty and the security of person.
The Canadian Bill of Rights guarantees the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property.
Those two documents also state that all human beings are equal before the law.
The proposed changes to the Criminal Code deny this equality, by giving to medical committees an arbitrary power which they do not want, an arbitrary power of life or death over as yet unborn human beings. They also go against the United Nations' declaration of the rights of the child which says that children have a right to our protection "before birth as well as after birth."
In Canada, the promoters of the campaign for abortion started a few years ago by asking only for limited changes in the law. One of these, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and I am quoting an elector in my county, once said before a parliamentary committee, in 1967 "that we should set a limit somewhere". Today, however, he is asking us to erase any mention of abortion in the Criminal Code.
Whatever the Minister of Justice may say and whatever his purpose may be, this government bill points to the way of no return.
Do you want to be responsible for putting our country on the way to abortion on request?
Abortion is a crime because it destroys human life. If you want to tolerate the destruction of human life for the benefit of another human being's health, why not do it for other reasons as well?
If you will admit abortion for health reasons, on the strength of what logic can you refuse legalized abortion on request?
Even in a pluralist society, the first duty of the state is to protect human life. When a bill goes against that principle, a member has the obligation of opposing it.
In the eyes of some members, the present government plans may seem erroneously

moderate. In fact, however, it has been proved that similar changes are only a first step. In Colorado, for instance, a similar act has led to a considerable increase in hospital abortions without reducing the number of illegal abortions. Moreover, this is but the start.
A few countries have passed even more permissive legislation, going as far as legalizing abortion on request. Almost all however started by legalizing abortion for so-called health reasons.
This is what was done in Sweden, in 1921. Later, in 1938, abortion for social reasons, "eugenics" and other reasons became possible. In 1946, the act became even more tolerant.
In Poland too, abortion was first legalized for vague medical reasons. In 1956, these reasons went so far as to include social reasons; today, in Poland, reasons for abortion are amongst the most permissive in the world.
Last year, the British permissive act came into effect as a result of a series of legal rulings which, in fact, legalized abortion for health reasons. The first of these rulings was given in 1938 and since, pressures have grown ceaselessly to legalize abortion on request.
Every argument in favour of broadening the laws on abortion is based on one or the other of the following assumptions: a) that the child that is not yet born is not a human being; b) that certain human beings have less value than others and, hence, that they can be sacrificed.
The proposed changes to our laws on abortion were defended as a compromise or accommodation solution. But when it is a question of fundamental values, there is no place for compromise, especially when nobody is forced to compromise. One of these fundamental values is the respect that we own human life itself.
What enlightened person would accept a compromise legislation authorizing execution without trial? This was, in certain places, a popular practice sanctioned by the conscience of the community. In this case, would a democratic government accept to legalize this kind of murder, if that is the wish of the local community?
What the government proposed is a law on abortion left to local interpretation, when it allows the killing of a human being for reasons of health which it feels need not be defined.

Since I was going to speak in a few minutes and I have a notion that I will lose my turn, I shall wait a little. I wanted to ask him a question then, but I will do it now.
When you were talking of the supreme sacrifice of a mother who must give her life for another life, would you be ready to do the same?

Mr. Speaker, this is a very good question. We do not have the opportunity to hear very often the hon. member for Mercier; he would rather whisper, but for once, he asked a logical question. I even tell him that I would be prepared to die because it is my role to defend the cause of Social Credit, which will ensure freedom and security to one and all.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to speak at any great length on this amendment. As a matter of fact, I am prompted to speak for only two reasons. My first reason is to make it clear on the record why I am voting against this bill. My second reason, also an important one, is to try to correct some possible misconceptions which may have arisen following the minister's statement yesterday. I refer to one portion of his statement as it appears at page 8575 of Hansard where the minister said:
I have drawn these matters to the attention of hon. members to emphasize the fact that, despite what has been said, where the amendments proposed before the standing committee that gave this bill detailed scrutiny were constructive and were improvements they were accepted by the government.
I am a member of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. It was my privilege to sit through practically all of the sessions during which this bill was discussed.
I have reviewed the minutes of the proceedings as they are reported and I find there were a total of 44 amendments submitted to the committee. The minister said yesterday there were 42, but I think if he rechecks he will find there were 44. Of the 44 amendments which were submitted, 30 were passed. It is interesting to note that of the 44 proposed amendments submitted to the committee, 28 were submitted by supporters of the government and 16 were submitted by members of

May 13, 1969
Criminal Code
this party. Of the 28 submitted by supporters of the government, 25 were allowed to pass. Of the 16 submitted by members of our party, only 5 were allowed to pass. I have examined the 28 amendments that were submitted by government supporters and I find, they were very minor. I think everyone is prepared to admit that the gut issues under discussion before the committee with respect to this bill involved the sections dealing with abortion and homosexuality.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Is he prepared to recognize that the statistics he has cited indicate that members of the government party did their homework in preparation for the study of this bill?

I am not so naive to believe that was the reason these amendments were passed. I have not been in this house very long, but I have been in politics long enough to realize just what goes on within the government caucus. The real issues in this bill were the clauses which dealt with abortion and homosexuality. Twelve of the 16 amendments submitted by our party dealt with these gut issues. I suggest that is the reason they were not adopted and were defeated by the government majority on that committee. I am not finding fault with the committee system. As a matter of fact, I want to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie) who chaired the committee. He did an exceptionally fine job and was very fair in his rulings. I find no fault with the committee system and I am not complaining about it. I am merely pointing out that the 28 amendments submitted by government supporters were minor amendments. Not one of them dealt with what I call the real gut issues of this bill.
I agree that one of our amendments, introduced by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), was adopted by the committee. Of the 16 submitted by our party, only 5 were allowed. I have worked it out on a percentage basis. Of the amendments submitted by government members, 89 per cent were passed by the government majority on the committee and only 31 per cent of those submitted by our party were passed. As I say, of the 16 amendments submitted by our party 12 dealt with what I consider to be the gut issues of the bill, but only one of them was allowed to pass.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit another question? Will
IMr. McQuaid.]
he admit with respect to the amendments which were proposed by government members, which I will not admit were merely minor, that they gained the support not only of government members on the committee but pretty uniformly of members from all parties on the committee?

I think that is a fair statement, Mr. Speaker, although I must say that some of the amendments submitted by government members were passed on division. However, to my way of thinking the most significant thing is that all of the amendments dealing with the gut issues of the bill, with the exception of one, were defeated by the government majority on the committee.
On the very first day the committee met, March 4, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacEwan) moved a motion that the committee agree to prepare and make four separate reports in relation to (a) abortion, (b) homosexuality and gross indecency, (c) lotteries and gambling and (d) all the remaining clauses. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, in all fairness why was that motion not allowed? If it had been a lot of the discussion we have been subjected to during the last 12 or 15 days could have been avoided. I suggest that his request was not unreasonable because if ever there was a bill introduced into this house that could be conveniently broken down into sections and reported in that way this was that bill. The suggestion of the hon. member for Central Nova provided a very convenient breakdown of the bill. If it had been accepted and if a free vote had been allowed, much of the discussion we are having today could have been avoided, and the house could be carrying on with other pending business which urgently needs to be dealt with. In all fairness to the committee system, I suggest that so far as the consideration of this bill was concerned the substantial amendments submitted by us had about as much chance of surviving as the proverbial snowball in hell.
Let me return briefly to the second reason which prompted me to enter the debate at this time. That reason is my desire to make it abundantly clear on the record why I cannot support the bill. I agree with many of the provisions of this bill. I would like to see many of them enacted as law because I think they are of substantial value to the people of Canada. I speak of such things as the tightening of the regulations with respect to firearms, the breathalyzer test, harassing telephone calls, bail, parole, our system of trial
May 13, 1969

by jury, and probation. These are all very-worth-while amendments and they are changes I would like to see incorporated in the law.
But the unfortunate part is that in order to approve these very commendable and worthwhile amendments I also have to vote approval of a law which, when enacted, will make a direct attack on human life, and this is why I cannot find myself able to do so. This is rather unfair. This is one of the reasons the bill should have been divided, so that I could have voted against those things with which I do not agree and voted for those parts of the bill which I would like to see enacted as law.
This bill has been called a high point in penal reform. Some portions of it do constitute a high point in penal reform, but I say that those portions which will make it easier to secure abortions are indeed a tragedy and represent the government's abdication of its responsibility for the protection of Canada's unborn citizens. Modern medicine and biology leave no reasonable doubt at all but that abortion does destroy human life. If somebody can satisfy me that abortion does not destroy human life, that to abort a woman even in the early weeks of pregnancy is not murder, then I would be inclined to think the other way. But everything I have read to date indicates without question of doubt that life does begin at conception. This has been attested to by every standard textbook on the subject that has been printed.
Many times during this debate the argument has been advanced that less stringent laws are needed in order to halt the traffic in illegal abortions or backroom butchery, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) called it the other day. Very lurid stories have been recounted of quack abortionists preying on innocent women at a staggering cost in maternal life. But I suggest that the facts are quite different. There is not a scrap of evidence to support the very inflated guesses, apparently used for their shock value, as to the number of illegal abortions and the deaths that result therefrom.
There are no statistics in which we can have confidence as to the number of criminal abortions performed in Canada, but we have statistics as to the number of deaths which occur as a result of criminal abortion. These statistics are prepared by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and I suggest they are reasonably accurate because on every certificate of death a doctor is required to state the
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion cause of death. From an examination of these statistics, Mr. Speaker, one can see that for the years 1964, 1965 and 1966 the number of deaths in all Canada by reason of illegal abortions was only 27.
I share the concern of some hon. members over the fact that there are some illegal abortions. I do not think we can deny this. But I submit that the provisions of this bill are not necessarily going to stop them, and this is conclusively proven by the figures obtained from those countries where abortion has already been legalized. As a matter of fact, on the contrary there is evidence that permissive laws increase the number of illegal abortions rather than cut them down. If you want an example all you have to do is to look at what is taking place in Hungary.
The argument is also advanced that by widening the laws on abortion we will improve the status of women. This argument was advanced by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway. I seriously suggest to hon. members that you do not improve the status of women by destroying the rights of other human beings, and when we widen the laws on abortion this is actually what we are doing. We are endangering the lives of other human beings because, as I say, it has been conclusively proven by medical evidence that a foetus is a living human being, and I suggest that to destroy it is nothing more or less than cold-blooded murder. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say that it will be a dark day for Canada when this proposed amendment passes, as I presume it will pass by reason of the large government majority.

duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the house that the questions to be raised at the time of adjournment tonight are as follows: the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave)-Air Canada-strike of mechanics-availability of alternative modes of travel; the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir)-Shipping-change in registration of Cape Breton Miner; the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose)- Post Office Department-Prince Rupert- monitoring telephone calls.
Criminal Code

May 13, 1969
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner that Bill C-150, to amend the Criminal Code, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act, the Prisons and Reformatories Act and to make certain consequential amendments to the Combines Investigation Act, the Customs Tariff and the National Defence Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, be read the third time and do pass, and the amendment of Mr. Matte.

Mr. Speaker, after long discussion, and interesting exchange of views, we are nearing the time when we shall have to make a decision regarding the bill under consideration.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, we should try to do away with emotionalism and appeal, to reason, if possible.
I do not for a moment suppose that my decision is the only one that might have been made on that legislation. I do not delude myself into the belief either that I have the monopoly of truth, and I am ready to accept the arguments of those who take a different view of this legislation.
Even if we do not share the same political allegiance, we should have enough respect for each other to realize that we are here for the same purpose, that is, to help the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, in the next minutes, I should like to give you the reasons which, in my opinion, may explain the choice 1 shall have to make. So as to avoid any misunderstanding I must say that I am a Catholic, a practising Catholic not as perfect perhaps as I should be, and not always setting the example as I should, but as a church-goer, I recognize in the house that the Catholic doctrine as set forth by Vatican II is quite clear. In fact, it boils down to this: Life must be safeguarded with extreme care from the very moment of conception. Any direct destruction of life in the mother's womb is immoral. No civil law can change the moral law which we must obey.
Mr. Speaker, it should be recognized, I believe, that the bill under study raises several moral problems. And at this time we have to ask ourselves whether we are in this house
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
to protect some religion, to endorse some beliefs, or to pass legislation.
This question, Mr. Speaker, can be readily answered. We are here to vote pieces of legislation. In some respects, they may come in conflict with the religious beliefs of some people. Yet, it is then we have the opportunity, faced with different opinions and beliefs, to stand united and cast aside our partisanship and our intolerance towards other Canadians who do not share our views.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is time we made some sincere effort and showed that we want Canada to extend from sea to sea, a country where people will have the right to live according to the beliefs they think are the best.
I have followed the debate with great interest and I feel that my friends from the Ralliement creditiste cannot accuse me of having turned a deaf ear to them.
I admit, Mr. Speaker, as a representative of a Quebec constituency, that I was proud at times to see people from my own province who were able to rise and deal eloquently and convincingly with such an important subject and thereby show that there still exist people willing to defend themselves and above all, to fight for moral principles.
However, I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that my admiration may have stopped there. I would have hoped that the members of the Ralliement creditiste would have made this essential distinction, between religion and the law, between sin and crime.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the intervention made a moment ago by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Ricard) who, in a few sincere words has given us the answer to all the objections raiced by the opposition. He said in a flight of oratory that he could not distinguish between religion and the law and that therefore he had to leave the matter to the religious authorities.
Mr. Speaker, when one mixes religion and the law, one shirks one's responsibilities as a legislator.
Mr. Speaker, I have wondered whether as a Christian legislator, I should vote for or against what the Church approves or disapproves.
Consequently, I attempted to make some research in order to find documents that might enlighten me and help me to take a honest decision, a decision consistent with an opinion of my own, arrived at with the help of serious works of reference.
May 13, 1969

Thus, I chanced upon a statement made in 1966 by English bishops and concerning abortion. After giving a brief summary of the Catholic doctrine of which I spoke a moment ago, here is an excerpt from this text, and I quote:
A number of citizen do not accept the Catholic position. We do not doubt their sincerity and we understand perfectly their wish to bring to the present legislation amendments that would protect women against those who are called "back-alley abortionists".
Catholics do not want their convictions to become the law of the land. They only ask that doctors, nurses and those who could be affected by the bill, should not be requested to act against their conscience.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that when my friends of the Ralliement Creditiste are trying-quite sincerely I know-to force their views upon us, they are going much farther than the bishops themselves..
I have already stated that I was against abortion and against any measure which could encourage homosexuality in any way. I was basing my opinion on moral and religious grounds. I am still of the same opinion.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I have carried my research further and I found two texts from which I would like to quote a few excerpts. I believe they have helped me reach a decision. The first is taken from a document prepared by a committee of theologians of Laval and was published in the June 13, 1968 issue of L'Eglise du Quebec. This is a summary of what it say:
Civil law must serve the commonweal of the body politic. It must undoubtedly draw its inspiration from the fundamental imperatives of unwritten law, but it cannot adjust itself to them to the extent of prescribing all that is relevant to it and of forbidding all that is contrary to it. In other words, political commonweal does not require that every moral fault be considered as a violation of the law.
It must also be pointed out that a so-called permissive law may be preferable to a limitative law if it promotes the commonweal while respecting the various religious faiths, opinions, mental habits or customs.
Finally, another part of this text seems to apply more particularly to the present case. It is said and I quote:
All citizens do not share the same opinions on morality standards. The legislator does not legislate for a given group, but for the whole political community. It follows that we can, as a matter of conscience, as Catholics, disapprove amoral acts while admitting that a legislation which condones them may be justified.
Criminal Code
The second text I would like to quote, and which also seems to give us general guidelines on the decision we have to make is the evidence given by the Canadian Catholic Conference before the standing committee on health, welfare and social affairs. I will not quote the whole evidence, but only extracts which helped me to answer the question I posed myself as a Christian legislator: Whai should be my position about that bill?
I quote:
To place the role of the legislator in its true perspective, and avoid any misunderstanding, we will call upon the teachings of the recent Vatican II Council-
-This Constitution is predicated upon a simple and evident truth, that the same persons are at the same time members of the religious community, the Church, and of the political community. The political community and the Church are both "at the service of the personal and social calling of the same men."
The ideal then is that they should seek for the good of all a sound co-operation, taking into consideration the circumstances of time and place.
I continue with the quotation.
The Church is aware that its role and responsibilities are totally different from those of the political community. It is thus important that members of the congregation always clearly distinguish "between the actions they take in their own name, as citizens, alone or as a group, and the actions they take in the name of the Church in agreement with their pastors."
However, in the political community-according to the teachings of the Council-Christians must act in their own name, as citizens."
In view of the economy of salvation itself, members of the congregation will learn to distinguish clearly between the rights and duties which fall on them as members of the Church and those which lie with them as members of the human society.
Here is a quotation which seems to me, Mr. Speaker,-with all due respect-very much to the point.
I go on with the quotation:
Besides-is it even necessary to stress the point- the teachings of the Church do not pervade the technical aspects of social and political matters. It still remains the responsibility of the legislators to devise concrete means to adopt their convictions to the often complex situations of daily life. They must not wait passively for the Church to come to their rescue in this regard; but on the contrary, they must-in co-operation with their colleagues- seek effective means to promote the commonweal, more particularly through the drafting and the enactment of wise and fair laws.
In the light of the texts of Vatican II that I have just quoted, the answer to the question I asked at the beginning of my remarks
86S2

May 13, 1969
Criminal Code
seems to me obvious enough. As a matter of fact, I find it further in the quotation:
A Christian legislator must make his own decisions. The criterion of his actions as a legislator is not first and foremost the interest of a religious group, but rather the commonweal.. . Members of Parliament have a temporal responsibility. They may vote, and in practice they often do, according to what the Church prohibits or approves, because the things prohibited or approved by the Church are often closely related to the common good.
But they have no obligation to do so.
Mr. Speaker, I think that faced by the rules of conduct laid down by the Bishops, I feel quite at liberty to state before this house that even if I am not in favour of the moral and religious aspects of the two most controversial parts of this bill I can, as a Canadian member of a pluralistic society and out of respect for those who do not share my religious beliefs, allow them to use a legislation which they find to their advantage.
I do not think that this leglislation, as the minister said, will be forced upon anybody in our constituencies. It will remain optional and left to the decision of the individual.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think that my religion forces me, to say to a pregnant woman who does not share my religious beliefs but who thinks she has a right to get an abortion: "You are not a Roman Catholic, I will not allow that law to help you".
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I think that in dealing with homosexuality, it was not mentioned that in spite of the amendments, gross indecency is still a criminal act which may be punished by five years in jail.
And the amendment which will enable consenting adults to do certain acts in private, only confirms the inviolability of private life. When the attention of the members of this house is drawn to the cases in which such a principle has led to inevitable abuses, too much stress is put on isolated facts, which may unfortunately be too numerous, this may cause us to forget the principle upon which all the people in this house agree upon, namely that the private life of people is sacred.
Everything that happens in private is not necessarily moral, but the law, and especially the Criminal Code, must not be brought into play. People must certainly keep on following the dictates of their conscience, so that this act will not become overly permissive.
It is obvious that this act will have to be used in moderation and construed in the most restrictive manner.

Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote the conclusion of an editorial by Mr. Claude Ryan in Le Devoir of April 23, 1969:
In a few words, Mr. Ryan gives us some guidelines in connection with the bill which seem to me very appropriate, and I quote:
Human law may allow many things, and, all things considered, it is better that it should allow more than less.
But the real criterium of the human life is still the conscience of the citizens rather than the law. We may always, if we are not satisfied with that legislation, continue to act according to our conscience. It is at that level that we finally find the quality of a civilization.
I therefore believe, Mr. Speaker, that I have stated some grounds serious enough to indicate to the members of this house that I am firmly convinced that with that basic distinction between morals and the law, the Canadians can apply a legislation which they consider right.
The future will tell us the results of that action. I think that we belong to a government which was elected, because the people were confident that we would take forwardlooking action and decisions, in short, that we would assume our responsibilities instead of dilly-dallying three or six months.
When we were elected, the population knew that we would adopt this legislation. I think it is my duty to endorse this policy but I repeat what I said earlier: from a moral point of view I accept the religious teachings. I find it said that we must choose among the various moral convictions of Canadians, but we have to consider the beliefs of the majority of Canadians and the previous votes of the house.
I confess, Mr. Speaker, that I waited to see what would be the results of the previous votes on abortion and homosexuality. They clearly indicate that a great majority of members of the house voted for abortion and for what is called homosexuality, but what, in fact is a measure to protect the private life of people.
From what I learnt, I have to convince myself that I live, not in a province, but in a country, that I have to accept its customs and beliefs and that I may, while having strong moral reservations, give the government a support which I hope will be of some use.
I shall not be among those who will hide behind the curtains when the vote comes. I do not think my constituents would be proud
May 13, 1969

of me if I decided to be away and to take a long trip at the time of voting.
I shall be there and shall vote as I feel best. It may be a mistake but at least I shall have the courage to take a stand after having duly pondered over it and considered some aspects of the question.
I now take advantage of the circumstances to congratulate the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) for his way of dealing with the government members while the bill was under consideration. I am one of those who, at a certain time, have voted against an amendment the hon. Minister of Justice had approved. That amendment was rejected and the minister accepted this decision. This proves that freedom does indeed exist, inside the Liberal party. We are subject to attacks which, I think, are unfair. The Minister of Justice has done a very good job indeed and if the law is passed, I think it will help to improve the condition of every Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, I have some short comments to make on two or three of the more controversial aspects of the bill. First of all I should like to speak for a few minutes on abortion. I will not put forward any ideas or enter into a discussion of the philosophy underlying abortion or whether or not it should be legalized. In my experience, which has been considerable in this field, there are two groups of people: Those who are in favour of legalizing abortion and those who are against it. There is no middle ground. We can only say that both sides tolerate each other. I may say that I belong to the group of people who believe that abortions should be permitted under certain circumstances.
I should like to congratulate the minister on making changes to the bill as it came from the committee and, specifically, on changing the definition of a hospital where abortions may be performed by the addition of the words, "approved hospitals". This is a good change because without it a good many Canadians would not have been able to have this service at a hospital of their choice, since not every hospital is necessarily accredited. It might well be that the term "accredited hospital" should have been entirely removed.
I should like also to comment on the establishment of an abortion committee consisting of three members. I feel this is unnecessarily cumbersome and is not in the best interests of Canadians. Having decided that abortions
Criminal Code
should be legalized, and they have always been legal under certain circumstances, we are now setting up a cumbersome mechanism to control them. Previously, most hospitals required an attending physician plus a consultant in good standing to rule on whether or not abortions should be performed. At present in all hospitals there are standards committees, which are becoming more highly organized, to guard against deviations from normal practice. Any physician who tends to perform what is considered to be too many abortions is. told that his standards are too lenient. Under the proposed law there will be a three man abortion committee, apart from the attending physician who looks after the patient. This is a very cumbersome method because it involves so many people. As a general rule in medicine consultations are taken between two doctors, and this works quite well. The addition of two more doctors will result in complications and a duplication of functions. I suppose the idea behind this provision is that it would be best for three people not associated with the patient or the physician to decide whether or not an abortion should be performed. However, I should point out that there is nothing to indicate that three people will do any better than the two normally required, namely the physician who knows the patient and his consulting colleague. The medical efficacy of such a method is open to question. I would also like to point out that the fact the attending physician is not to be a member of the committee means that the person who knows best whether or not an abortion should be carried out will have no say in the matter.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
So, I feel that this is a retrograde step which will not be in the best interests of the patient. Under modern medical practice the lives of very few patients are endangered by abortions, although the opposite has been argued. There are, however, a great many places which fall within this terminology "endangering a patient's health". Here, many factors need to be taken into consideration; it is a matter of relativity. I feel the transfer of responsibility from the patient's own physician to an abortion committee is not a good step from a purely medical point of view. The committee procedure now suggested is necessarily cumbersome and makes it harder to arrive at a decision. This, to some extent, endangers the life of a patient and it certainly increases the complications which may arise. Abortions should be carried out before the

May 13, 1969
Criminal Code
eighth week of pregnancy has been completed. From a practical point of view very little time is provided for a patient to present herself, have a bed found for her in a hospital and collect three people to decide whether or not it would be in her interest to carry out an abortion. Physicians are busy people; they move around a great deal in hospitals and outside them, and many of them are away at any given time.
Delay in carrying out this procedure would no doubt lead to some increase in mortality and to a considerably greater increase in morbidity, or associated complications. In my opinion, abortion committees will not function well in practice. It is well known that bad laws are always circumvented and then to become sealed off to prevent them from causing too much difficulty. I feel the abortion committees will take either a hard line or a soft line approach. I am inclined to think that for practical purposes the procedure will often consist of the patient signing a consultation form on her way past the hospital desk and that much of the value which the Department of Justice no doubt believes this amendment to contain will be lost. As I say, the committees will probably not function very well in practice and it might have been better to have retained the original idea of acting on the advice of a physician and one consulting colleague. In countries such as Sweden, where liberal abortion laws exist, complications are considerably higher in areas in which cumbersome abortion committees have to be consulted.
Then again, cumbersome abortion laws tend to discourage patients from seeking care along ethical medical lines; they tend to gravitate to the so-called criminal abortionists -abortionists who are often very good from a purely medical point of view. As a society I am sure we would like to have these patients cared for in our hospitals where those who are entitled to receive this service will be able to do so under the control of reasonable laws. My own feeling is that this abortion committee arrangement is too cumbersome. There is no evidence that it will lead to a reduction in numbers of abortions. In the case of country hospitals it will be difficult to find four physicians to fulfil this function, particularly since many of them do not feel they are able to serve on such committees.
In essence, the legislation before us brings about no significant change in the abortion laws apart from the provision for setting up these committees. Nothing has been said about population control, a subject which I 
believe we shall eventually have to consider. Nor does the bill permit abortion at the request of the women concerned-something which various groups in our society consider to be reasonable.
Again, this new abortion law does not in any way increase the chances of abortions being performed. There is no reason to suppose the number of abortions will be greater in future than those already being carried out in accordance with certain ethical standards. Perhaps the necessity of abortion laws draws attention to the failure of our society to prevent unwanted pregnancies. Perhaps the legislation which has recently been introduced in this field will do much more to look after the problem than either this bill or the discussion which has taken place during the last week or so. The piece of legislation we are considering does not in any way alter the indications for abortion, while making it much more cumbersome to have abortions carried out. Indeed, the amendment concerning abortion might well have been left in abeyance for all the value it really represents.
I should like to speak for a few moments, now, on the breathalizer test proposal which has been hailed as a great advance by many people. In England, presumably, such a provision was very effective in cutting down the number of accidents, and the introduction of the system into this country has received widespread support.
I am in agreement with this proposal but at the same time I do not believe we can expect it to have any marked effect in cutting down the number of accidents. I would refer hon. members to a news item which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of April 5, 1969, under a London dateline. This article reads:
^ The ministry of transport has reported a heavy increase in road accidents and the worst monthly toll of deaths and injuries since breath tests for suspected drunken drivers were introduced 16 months ago.
Provisional figures hurriedly published in advance of the Easter weekend disclosed that 600 people died on the roads in January, 102 more than in the same month last year. The total casualties were 27,700, a rise of 3,815.
"People are less frightened than they were of the breath tests," said a spokesman for the automobile association. "At first they thought policemen would be waiting round every corner. Now they know they aren't-and driving standards have fallen."
I would therefore caution those who feel the introduction of breathalyzer tests will improve our driving standards. I think their main value will be found at the scene of
May 13, 1969

accidents in deciding on allocation of blame. With these concluding remarks, Mr. Speaker, I shall resume my seat.

speechtext:
It being six o'clock I do now leave the chair until 8 p.m.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, the third last speaker, the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. McQuaid), pointed out that in the committee several amendments were introduced by members of the government and passed, but that few of those introduced by members of the opposition passed. As a member of that committee I wish to say that I felt all reasonable proposals passed.
Some of them did not pass for two reasons. The majority of the amendments that dealt with abortion were, I suggest, not really amendments at all but sought effectively to destroy the purpose of the abortion provisions. If those particular motions dealing with the abortion provisions had been accepted, I suggest our law would have been placed 120 years behind the times. The social legislation of this country would have been made to appear rather backward. A period when we are rethinking the basis for legislative interference with individual freedom is no time for a particular group to try to impose their personal beliefs on the rest of the nation.
I wish to speak on some of the principles that are involved in this bill. First, I should like to deal with the breathalyzer provisions contained in clause 16. Although I have spoken in the house and in committee in favour of many of the amendments, and intend to support the bill on third reading, I am gravely concerned about the lack of protection for the individual in certain parts of the bill. I ask myself: Is it sufficient for us to believe that very few will be incorrectly convicted under these provisions?
Under the new section 222, which is commonly referred to as the ability impaired section, one may be charged with the indictable offence of driving a motor vehicle while one's ability to do so is impaired by alcohol. Upon conviction for this offence one may be fined
Criminal Code
up to $500 or imprisoned for up to three months, or both.
Under the new section 223, which is the section that makes the breathalyzer test mandatory, a police officer may, if he believes that the driver of a vehicle is committing or has committed an offence under the ability impaired section, demand that the driver take a breathalyzer test.
The proposed section 224 deals with the weight given to the reading resulting from the breathalyzer test and provides that, if such test reading indicates that the alcohol in the blood exceeds 80 milligrams of alcohol in 100 millitres of blood, the accused is guilty of an offence and liable to a fine of up to $1,000, to imprisonment up to six months, or both.
Now, what can happen? I have worked out some examples to demonstrate my proposition. If one is charged with having one's ability impaired, the evidence of the prosecution could be that of the arresting officer, who would probably say that from his observation made at the scene of the accident the driver appeared to be impaired. This would be supported by the breathalyzer test, which gave a reading, say, of .09 grams.
By way of defence, the accused could call the evidence, say, of three witnesses to confirm that he consumed only one ounce of alcohol up to the time of the accident, and that he behaved in a completely normal manner.
If the judge believed that evidence, he would accept as a fact that the accused had consumed only one ounce of alcohol, and thus, by implication, he would disbelieve the evidence produced by the machine. In other words, if the accused and his witnesses were believed, the accused could be acquitted, the inference being that the operator of the machine had erred in his testing technique or that the machine was defective.
An arresting officer could, and in many cases would, lay charges under both sections^-that is to say, the ability impaired section and the breathalyzer section-for the obvious purpose of obtaining a conviction under the latter should the accused be acquitted under the former. Both charges would be tried together in the usual way, and the same evidence would apply.
Consequently, the judge could very well find himself in this impossible situation: that while he acquitted the accused on the first charge of ability impaired because he found as a fact that the man had consumed only one

May 13, 1969
Criminal Code
ounce of alcohol, and that therefore his ability was not impaired, he would have no choice but to convict on the second charge because the evidence as to the amount of alcohol consumed and the driver's condition would not be relevant. In other words, the court would be powerless to relieve under the section; the machine would be all powerful. This situation could not help but bring justice into disrepute because an acquittal on the first charge necessarily discredited the breathalyzer test which was relied upon on the second charge for a conviction.

Let us suppose the same person or his friend who knows the story is picked up one month later under the same circumstances as just described; that is to say, the driver had consumed one ounce of alcohol and had become involved in an accident. The arresting constable advises him that he is to be charged with ability impaired under Section 222 and demands a breathalyzer test under Section 223. This time the accused, remembering the earlier conviction based upon the findings of the breathalyzer, simply refuses to take the test. For this refusal he is charged under Section 223. That is, for failing to take the test he could be found guilty of an offence and fined up to $1,000, or imprisoned for up to six months, or both. Let us say he refuses to take the test because he believed the operator to be incompetent, the machine to be defective, or both. He is now worse off. Section 224a provides that if he refuses without reasonable excuse to take the test the court may draw an inference from that refusal which is adverse to the accused. This evidence by way of inference could very well cause the magistrate to disbelieve the evidence of the accused or his witnesses that he had only one drink. He could then accept the evidence of the constable and convict the accused under Section 222 and, again, under Section 223(2) for failing to take the test. The result would be, Mr. Speaker, that the breathalyzer test, supported as it is by Section 224, would have been all powerful and indirectly would have brought about two convictions because of the attempt to avoid it. Is this not putting too much power in the hands of the arresting authority? At best it puts a premium on the evidence of the arresting constable and, perhaps, too much emphasis on the importance of a single scientific test.
Although I accept, and believe that the public is ready to accept, the philosophy of creating a statutory offence for operating a vehicle with a stated amount of alcohol in the
tMr. Chappell.]
body, just as it has accepted as an offence an infraction of an arbitrary speed limit, I believe that the evidentiary aspect is faulty. In our endeavour to improve safety on the highways we must be careful not to net the innocent. Can we be reasonably certain that there is sufficient protection for the unusual case and for the innocent? The consequences of an erroneous conviction could be most serious to an accused from an insurance, employment or social standpoint. Other innocent people could be affected. Suppose a man is convicted of ability impaired, mainly because the breathalyzer machine gave a reading of 0.09, and his insurance company denies liability under his insurance policy. It may be that claimants against him for injuries arising out of a collision are unable to recover the full amounts of their just claims. It could also be that the breathalyzer was in error, but because the accused was detained for some hours he was powerless to be examined by other witnesses or to arrange for some other type of chemical test to refute the breathalyzer test.
I believe the breathalyzer is subject to error and, in some cases, serious error because of lack of skill or care by the operator or defect in the machine, as evidenced by the fact that it is customary to take two or three tests several minutes apart. I believe the accused should in all cases be given the opportunity to be provided with a sample of his urine or blood for a comparative or backup test.
Dr. R. N. Rabinovitch, a medical doctor and renowned authority on the subject, who gave evidence before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in November, 1966 holds that it is wrong for the blood alcohol level to be determined by analysis of breath only. The late Dr. Ward Smith, who was then an expert with the Department of the Attorney General for the province of Ontario, in his letter to Dr. Rabinovitch on May 10, 1965 when referring to the consideration that the blood level should be determined by analysis of breath only stated:
I am sure that you would deplore the situation;
I do, possibly for different reasons.
Under British legislation the breathalyzer test is used as a screening test; that is to say, the reading indicates whether the arresting authorities should demand a blood or urine test. In England, after considerable original research, the Highway Safety Act made it a statutory offence to drive a vehicle with a certain amount of alcohol in the body. There
May 13, 1969

has been a reduction of accidents but more care was taken to protect innocent people.
The Canadian Bar Association, after lengthy study, some of it in conjunction with the Canadian Medical Association, recommended the use of the breathalyzer for purposes of prima facie evidence. However, they recommended the individual be given protection by making it mandatory that he be supplied with a sample of his breath and, in addition, that he be entitled upon request to a sealed sample of his own blood or urine. The Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, which received many briefs and heard many witnesses, in its fifth report to the House of Commons on February 9, 1967, recommended among other things that there should be legislation making it unlawful for anyone with a blood level of 0.08 per cent to drive a motor vehicle; that the blood level should be determined by an analysis of breath, with the provision that at the request of the accused there be blood and urine tests as confirmation. In addition the Committee recommended that the accused be offered a sample of the material; and, further, that all witnesses who had anything to do with the testing and handling of the sample should be available for cross-examination at the trial of the accused.
I believe it to be universally acknowledged by all experts that the breathalyzer operator should not rely upon one sample of breath only. The custom may be developed to take two or three samples, but the legislation does not so provide. Further, under Section 224, although the accused has the right to be supplied with a specimen of his own breath, there is no provision for the sealing or handling of that sample. Because the accused or another could tamper with this unsealed sample the court, of necessity, would be most suspicious of an analysis carried out by the accused. For example, there is nothing to stop the accused or his friends from breathing into the bag after the accused has taken the test. As I say, the court of necessity would be most suspicious of an analysis carried out by the accused.
I believe it would have been better for us to provide that in the event the accused is detained for more than one hour-thus preventing him from arranging for his own test-the arresting authorities offer facilities for a sample of his urine or blood to be taken and preserved for him. Surely, the provision for such a further test would induce the operator of the breathalyzer machine to use utmost care.
Criminal Code
This safeguard need not be unduly cumbersome or expensive. The arresting authorities would simply be required to offer the accused facilities for the taking of either a urine or blood sample and to hold the same for up to 48 hours in order to give the accused time to retain a solicitor and carry out whatever test might be deemed advisable. The arresting authorities should have the choice as to whether it would be urine or blood because, in many cases, a doctor would not be available to take the blood. Granted blood would be better, but in many cases it would be difficult to obtain. It would be up to the solicitor for the accused to create the chain of evidence in respect of the handling and testing of the sample. It is said by acknowledged experts that the blood test is subject to only a 5 per cent error and the urine test only a 10 per cent error, if properly carried out. Generally, both tests are more reliable than a single breath test.

I appreciate the fact that under the proposed legislation the accused might be offered a sample of his own breath, but is one sample sufficient? It is most difficult to provide for sealing. If this is done, over the next few months we will collect some statistics to assist us in determining	whether the
breathalyzer is always reliable.
In conclusion, may I say in all other respects I enthusiastically support the bill. I regret the delay of its passage through this house.

I have spoken several times on some of the amendments. I have spoken as best I could, using all the arguments at our disposal. First of all, I will not separate man from his religion although some claim that the law should be separated from religion. We have pleaded religious as well as scientific arguments. We set forth as proof the testimonials of renowned doctors. I did not have the opportunity to sit on the committee but I believe that out of the 44 amendments moved, 30 were passed. Moreover, 89 percent of those 30 amendments had been submitted by Liberals. I do not know exactly what happened, but when we hear, for instance, another member confess that those amendments were all adopted by the committee by a majority-he did say by a majority, and he was right to say so-we realize that a strong majority on the committee was in favour of the bill.
As a matter of fact, if we consider the committee, the representatives of the N.P.D. and the Liberals made up a strong majority, and when the smaller group, on the other side wanted to object, they still were a 100 per cent majority.
All this should make it clear that a majority in the committee does not mean a majority of the people. I submit that the committee did not necessarily represent the majority of the people. And that is why we are opposed to the bill.
To start with, unfortunately the bill was not divided and we shall have to vote against the whole package. Had it been split, the debate would have been much more straightforward and sincere.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because for many years the maintenance of safety on the highways has been part of my duties as a police officer. I hasten to add that I have no doubt whatsoever that the misuse of alcohol
Criminal Code
is one of the main causes of the high rate of death on our highways. It is not the only cause. Perhaps the prime cause is the general disregard for human life which is only too prevalent in our society. The wonderful opportunities we have to enjoy the full life, only too often are frustrated by carelessness. Alcohol is one of those things which dims a finer perception of our opportunities. There is no question at all in the minds of many of us who saw the wonderful film which was shown to the members of the committee and others concerning the disastrous effects of the misuse of alcohol on a person's ability to control an automobile.
It has been one of the prime facets of British and Canadian justice that we give the benefit of the doubt to the accused. I would like, therefore, to see the permitted level of alcohol set at one one-thousandth or .1 per cent. This would eliminate many arguments that we have heard that we should give the driver the benefit of the doubt. Some people think that they are in control of themselves after they have had a number of beers or a number of double whiskies. Be that as it may, there is no doubt at all, according to the film, that when you have .08 per cent of alcohol in your blood you are impaired. I would like to go that much further and say that we should set it at the nice round figure of .1 per cent, then all doubt whatsoever would be eliminated. This would be fair play taken to a very fair point. You would not have to worry whether your cough medicine had an alcoholic content, whether you had eaten more Christmas dinner than usual, or whether you had lost track of one drink.
I do not speak from hearsay. As I said, for some 15 years it was my job to be intimately connected with the results of the misuse of alcohol. I went out after the complaint came in; after the empty bottles were thrown out into the ditches and after most of the evidence was gone except for the wreckage. All that remained was the dead bodies and the sight of those people who might never walk again or who might never again have the proper use of their limbs. It is certain that the wreckage of automobiles and of public and personal property is immense. I hate to have to remind hon. members that the loss of human life in this great democracy of ours amounts to some 5,500 lives a year, more people by far than have lost their lives in all the wars since Canada entered Confederation. This is a disgrace to us.
So I am glad to see that this amendment to the Criminal Code is attempting to fill this

May 13, 1969
Criminal Code
terrible gap in our law and. to put some real teeth into our law. However, let me say again that I would like to remove all doubt about the permitted amount of alcohol in the blood when driving by setting it at a figure of .1 per cent. Then, there would be no argument about it whatsoever. If the police were able to establish that you did have this percentage of alcohol in your blood, there would hardly be any need for more evidence before the courts.
Some people argue that breathalyzers or blood tests are an invasion of our privacy. I am inclined to agree with that. But I must say that if one were to weigh the right to privacy against the terrible toll of human life, then I am sure that those of us who think we should drive with reasonable care and regard for other people believe that this small invasion of our privacy is well worth giving up if we are to remove this blight of modern civilization from our highways which results in the loss of the lives of hundreds and thousands of people.
So, I add my one small voice to those in favour of the better features of this bill. These people have put a great deal of time and effort into the preparation of these amendments in the standing Committee. I think we should certainly give them a fair chance. If we find that this law is too severe, it should be toned down. I believe that at present there is something seriously wrong in the law. I think we must take a bold step forward and make sure that people who murder on the highways are no longer permitted to do so by sloppy laws, by weak courts and by a poor administration of the law.
Here, I would like to add one or two words of warning. It is not good enough to have stringent laws; it is not good enough to have a well thought out and a well meaning Criminal Code setting down the permitted percentage of alcohol in the blood unless there is a police force which is well trained and respected to enforce those provisions.
